'''Erik Gustav Elfving''' (25 June 1908 – 25 March 1984) was a [[Finland|Finnish]] [[mathematician]] and [[statistician]]. He wrote pioneering works in mathematical statistics, especially on the [[design of experiments]].<ref name="DMNP"/>

==Early life==
Erik Gustav Elfving was son of [[Fredrik Elfving]] (1854–1942), a professor of botany at the [[University of Helsinki]],<ref name="Puk430"/> and Thyra Elfving (née Ingman).<!-- p. 123 --><ref name="DMNP"  /> He was the youngest of four children.<!-- p. 123 --><ref name="DMNP"  /> Gustav Elfving earned excellent grades at the ''[[Svenska normallyceum i Helsingfors]]'', a Helsinki  [[Gymnasium (school)#North European countries|gymnasium]] for [[Swedish-speaking Finns|Swedish-speaking]] boys, from which he graduated in 1926.<ref>{{harvtxt|Nordström|1999|p=174}}</ref> In the same year he enrolled at the University of Helsinki, planning to major in astronomy. He switched to mathematics, graduating in 1930 in mathematics, with astronomy and physics as minor subjects. From 1927 to 1929, he worked as a computational assistant at the astronomical observatory of
the University of Helsinki.<ref name="Nord7576" >{{harvtxt|Nordström|1999|pp=175–176}}</ref> He studied [[probability theory]] under [[Jarl Waldemar Lindeberg|J. W. Lindeberg]],<ref name="Puk430"/> who is now known for [[Lindeberg's condition]] for the [[central limit theorem]].<ref>{{cite journal
| author=J. W. Lindeberg
| title=Eine neue Herleitung des Exponentialgesetzes in der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung
| year=1922 |journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift
| pages=211–225 |volume=15
| url=http://www-gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/cgi-bin/digbib.cgi?PPN266833020_0015}}</ref><!-- p. 124 --><ref name="DMNP"  /> He wrote his (1934) dissertation  under the supervision of [[Rolf Nevanlinna]];<ref name="Puk430"/> his thesis studied [[Riemann surfaces]] and their [[Uniformization theorem|uniformization]].<ref name="Nord75">{{harvtxt|Nordström|1999|p=175}}</ref> In the [[value distribution theory of holomorphic functions|Nevanlinna theory]] of the values of [[meromorphic function]]s, Elfving's results  were praised by Drasin<!--  1977, p. 85 -->.<ref name="DMNP"/><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Drasin | first1 = D | year = 1977 | title = The inverse problem of the Nevanlinna theory | journal = Acta Math. | volume = 138 | pages = 83–151 | doi=10.1007/bf02392314| doi-access = free }}</ref>

=== Fiancée's death and his 1935 expedition to Greenland ===
Elfving was engaged to a young woman, who died in 1935, probably from [[tuberculosis]]. The grieving parents of his fiancée helped Elfving contact the Danish Geodetic Institute, which hired him as the mathematician for a cartographic expedition
to Western Greenland in the summer of 1935.<ref name="Nord75"/> Elfving was photographed while he made [[theodolite]] measurements and peered from a tent.<ref name="Nord7576"/> Heavy rains forced the expedition to remain sheltered in their tents for three days, during which Elfving started to think about the best locations to take measurements for [[least squares]] estimation.<ref name="Nord76">{{harvtxt|Nordström|1999|p=176}}</ref>

==Statistical research==
[[File:Theb1982.jpg|thumb|right|alt=Picture of a man taking measurements with a theobolite in a frozen environment.|Gustav Elfving invented the [[optimal design|optimal design of experiments]], and so minimized surveyors' need for  [[theodolite|theodolite measurements]] ''(pictured)'', while trapped in his tent in storm-ridden [[Greenland]].<ref name="Nord76"/>]]
In [[statistics]], Elfving did research in the [[design of experiments]], [[probability theory]], and [[statistical inference]], as well as [[applied statistics|applications]].

===Optimal design of experiments===
In statistics, Elfving is known as one of the founders of the modern theory of the [[optimal design of experiments]].<ref name="DMNP">{{harvtxt|Draper|Mäkeläinen|Nordström|Pukelsheim|1999}}</ref><ref name="Puk430">{{harvtxt|Pukelsheim|2006|loc=Appendix of Biographies 2 Gustav Elfving 1908–1984, p. 430}}</ref><ref name="Fellman">{{harvtxt|Fellman|1999}}</ref> While accompanying a surveying expedition to western Greenland, extended and intense rains left Elving with three days in his tent, during which time he considered the best locations of observations to estimate parameters of linear models.<ref name="Puk430"/><ref name="Nord76"/><ref name="Fellman"/> Elfving's ideas appeared in his paper on the optimal design of experiments for estimating linear models. This paper also introduced concepts from [[convex geometry]], including "Elfving sets"<ref>{{harvtxt|Pukelsheim|2006|pp=43–44, 107, 134, 191, 231, 420}}</ref> and Elfving's theorem.<ref>{{harvtxt|Pukelsheim|2006|pp=50, 107, 182, 190, 198, 212, 231, 239, 259, 410, 422}}</ref><ref>Studden, W. J. Elfving's theorem and optimal designs for quadratic loss. ''Ann. Math. Statist.'' ''' 42 ''' (1971), 1613–1621. {{MR|341771}}</ref>  Being symmetric, ''Elfving sets'' are formed by the [[union (mathematics)|union]] of a set and its reflection through the origin, −''S''&nbsp;∪&nbsp;''S''.<ref>{{harvtxt|Pukelsheim|2006|pp=43–44}}</ref><ref>
* Elfving, G. (1953). Convex sets in statistics. In ''Tolfte Skandinaviska Matematikerkongressen'', Lund, August 10–15, 1953, 34–39.
* {{cite journal | last1 = Elfving | first1 = G | year = 1954b | title = Geometric allocation theory | journal = Skandinavisk Aktuarietidskrift | volume = 37 | pages = 170–190 }}
* {{cite journal | last1 = Elfving | first1 = G | year = 1957a | title = A selection problem in experimental design | journal = Societas Scientiarum Fennica Commentationes Physico-Mathematicae | volume = 20 | issue = 2| pages = 3–10 }}
* Elfving, G. (1957b). Minimax character of balanced experimental designs. In ''XIII Congr. Math. Scand.'' 69–76.
</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Fellman|1999|pp=198–199}}</ref> According to {{harvtxt|Chernoff|1999|p=204}}, Elfving was generous in crediting others' results: His paper in the [[Harald Cramér|Cramér]]-[[festschrift]] acknowledged unpublished notes of [[Leonard Jimmie Savage|L. J. Savage]]; Elfving was a referee for the fundamental paper on optimal designs by [[Jack Carl Kiefer|Kiefer]] and [[Jacob Wolfowitz|Wolfowitz]].<ref name="Chernoff204">{{harvtxt|Chernoff|1999|p=204}}</ref><ref name="KW">Kiefer, J.; Wolfowitz, J. Optimum designs in regression problems. ''Ann. Math. Statist.'' ''' 30 ''' 1959 271–294.   {{MR|104324}}</ref>

===Other statistical contributions===
As a Professor at the University of Helsinki, Elfving was responsible for writing [[Finnish language]] texts, which were used for decades. In his texts and reviews, Elfving emphasized the decision-theoretic foundations of statistics, following [[Jerzy Neyman|Neyman]], [[Egon Pearson|Pearson]], and [[Abraham Wald|Wald]], and recognized the value of [[Bayesian statistics|Bayesian methods]] in statistics and also in [[operations research]].<ref>Elfving, G. (1957b). Minimax character of balanced experimental designs. In ''XIII Congr. Math. Scand''. 69–76.</ref> Elfving introduced the statistical symbol for [[probabilistic independence]] ⊥⊥, which is a stronger condition than [[orthogonality]] ⊥, by the 1950s.<ref name="Nordstrom">{{harvtxt|Nordström|1999|p=177}}</ref>

Elfving made notable contributions in many fields. In mathematics, he did research in [[complex analysis]] and probability theory (particularly [[Markov process|Markov]] and [[point process]]es). In statistical theory, his most influential work was in optimal design, but he also worked in [[Statistical sampling|sampling theory]],<ref>
* Elfving, G. (1954a). A unified approach to the allocation problem in sampling theory. Abstract from ''Proc. Inter. Math. Congr.'', Amsterdam, Sept. 1954.
* {{cite journal | last1 = Elfving | first1 = G | year = 1954b | title = Geometric allocation theory | journal = Skandinavisk Aktuarietidskrift | volume = 37 | pages = 170–190 }}
* Elfving, G. (1956). Selection of nonrepeatable observations for estimation. ''Proc. Third Berkeley Symp. Math. Statist. Probab'' volume '''1''' pp. 69–75. Univ. California Press, Berkeley.</ref>
[[psychometrics]], [[applied statistics]], and the [[decision science]]s (including [[decision theory]], [[game theory]], and [[Bayesian statistics]]). He also contributed to [[mathematics education]] by writing textbooks, book reviews, and [[popular science]]. He wrote papers and a book on the [[history of mathematics]].<ref name="DMNP"/>

====Students====
He also supervised many students. [[Elja Arjas]] is known for his work on inference on stochastic processes and reliability theory, as well as for his supervision of Esa Nummelin and [[Hannu Oja]].<ref name="MGArjas">{{MathGenealogy|id=57096}}</ref> [[Johann Fellman]] has studied optimal designs for nonsingular or nondifferentiable information functions as well economic theory, and genetics (particularly the frequency of twin births) and for his supervision of Kenneth Nordström and [[Katarina Juselius]].<ref>Rosenqvist, G., Juselius, K., Nordström, K. and Palmgren, J. (eds.) "''A Spectrum of Statistical Thought. Essays in Statistical Theory, Economics and Population Genetics in Honour of Johan Fellman''", Publications of the Swedish School of Economics and Business Administration, 46, 1991</ref><ref name="MGNordstrom">{{MathGenealogy|id=20423}}</ref>  <!-- Anders Ekholm has been a Professor of Epidemiology in Stockholm, I think.  -->

==Academic and scientific offices==
[[File:Unioninkatu 34.jpg|thumb|right|alt=University of Helsinki (Main Building)|Elfving graduated from the University of Helsinki.]]
During 1938–1945, Elfving worked as a lecturer at the [[Helsinki University of Technology]].
During the academic year 1946–1947, Elfving served as ''locum tenens'' professor at Stockholm University. In 1948 Elfving became a Professor of Mathematics at the [[University of Helsinki]] succeeding [[Lars Ahlfors]], who had moved to Harvard University. Elfving visited [[William Feller]] at [[Cornell University]] in 1949 and 1950. He was an invited plenary speaker at the Third Berkeley Symposium on Probability and Mathematical Statistics in 1955. That same year, he visited Columbia University in the Spring, at the invitation of [[Theodore W. Anderson]], [[Herbert Robbins]], and [[Herbert Solomon]]. He visited Solomon again at Stanford University during the fall of 1960 and the spring of 1966.<!-- pp. 124-125 --><ref name="DMNP"  />

He was elected as a fellow of the [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]] in 1955 and an elected member of the [[International Statistical Institute]] in 1963. Elfving was elected <!-- on 10 April -->as a foreign member of the [[Swedish Academy of Sciences]] in 1974, the same year that he was elected to the [[Royal Statistical Society]].<ref name=Nord82>{{harvtxt|Nordström|1999|p=182}}</ref> He served on the editorial boards of three international journals: ''[[Probability Theory and Related Fields]]'' (1962–1975), ''[[Annals of Mathematical Statistics|The Annals of Mathematical Statistics]]'' (1964–1967), and ''[[Mathematica Scandinavica]]'' (1953–1972).<!-- p. 125-126 --><ref name=" DMNP"/> Elfving had a deep sense of honor and propriety: When he resigned from the editorial boards following decades of service, he requested that he not be sent complimentary issues of the journals; when he failed to accomplish high levels of research, he offered to return the funding to the granting agency.<ref name="Nord82"/>

At the University of Helsinki from 1964 to 1975, Elfving acted as the "[[Inspektor|inspector]]" of the [[Åbo Nation]], a [[Nations at Finnish universities#Swedish-speaking|Swedish-speaking]] [[University of Helsinki#Student nations|"nation" at the University of Helsinki]].<ref name="Nordstrom"/> In Finnish and Swedish universities, [[nations at Finnish universities|"nations"]] are  student associations with similarities to fraternities or cooperatives; the ''inspector'' is a highly respected university officer, usually a senior professor, who officiates and delivers addresses at formal functions.
